question: Which CAPEC patterns exploit weakness CWE-308, which ATT&CK techniques do they map to, and what mitigations apply?

answer.headline: Gathered 26 record(s) from 2 source(s); 14 cross-source correlation(s) on shared identifiers.
answer.narrative: The CAPEC patterns exploiting CWE-308 include Use of Known Domain Credentials (CAPEC-560), Try Common or Default Usernames and Passwords (CAPEC-70), Windows Admin Shares with Stolen Credentials (CAPEC-561), Rainbow Table Password Cracking (CAPEC-55), Use of Known Kerberos Credentials (CAPEC-652), Credential Stuffing (CAPEC-600), Password Spraying (CAPEC-565), Remote Services with Stolen Credentials (CAPEC-555), Use of Captured Hashes (Pass The Hash) (CAPEC-644), Password Brute Forcing (CAPEC-49), Kerberoasting (CAPEC-509), and Use of Captured Tickets (Pass The Ticket) (CAPEC-645). These map to MITRE ATT&CK techniques such as Valid Accounts (T1078), Default Accounts (T1078.001), SMB/Windows Admin Shares (T1021.002), Password Cracking (T1110.002), Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets (T1558), Credential Stuffing (T1110.004), Password Spraying (T1110.003), Remote Services (T1021), Remote Email Collection (T1114.002), External Remote Services (T1133), Pass the Hash (T1550.002), Password Guessing (T1110.001), Kerberoasting (T1558.003), and Pass the Ticket (T1550.003). Applicable mitigations for these techniques include Multi-factor Authentication (M1032), Password Policies (M1027), Account Use Policies (M1036), Privileged Account Management (M1026), and User Account Management (M1018).

records.name: Use of Known Domain Credentials
records.label: AttackPattern
records.description: An adversary guesses or obtains (i.e. steals or purchases) legitimate credentials (e.g. userID/password) to achieve authentication and to perform authorized actions under the guise of an authenticated user or service.

records.name: Try Common or Default Usernames and Passwords
records.label: AttackPattern
records.description: An adversary may try certain common or default usernames and passwords to gain access into the system and perform unauthorized actions. An adversary may try an intelligent brute force using empty passwords, known vendor default credentials, as well as a dictionary of common usernames and passwords. Many vendor products come preconfigured with default (and thus well-known) usernames and passwords that should be deleted prior to usage in a production environment. It is a common mistake to forget to remove these default login credentials. Another problem is that users would pick very simple (comm… (+201 chars)

records.name: Windows Admin Shares with Stolen Credentials
records.label: AttackPattern
records.description: An adversary guesses or obtains (i.e. steals or purchases) legitimate Windows administrator credentials (e.g. userID/password) to access Windows Admin Shares on a local machine or within a Windows domain.

records.name: Rainbow Table Password Cracking
records.label: AttackPattern
records.description: An attacker gets access to the database table where hashes of passwords are stored. They then use a rainbow table of pre-computed hash chains to attempt to look up the original password. Once the original password corresponding to the hash is obtained, the attacker uses the original password to gain access to the system.

records.name: Use of Known Kerberos Credentials
records.label: AttackPattern
records.description: An adversary obtains (i.e. steals or purchases) legitimate Kerberos credentials (e.g. Kerberos service account userID/password or Kerberos Tickets) with the goal of achieving authenticated access to additional systems, applications, or services within the domain.

records.name: Credential Stuffing
records.label: AttackPattern
records.description: An adversary tries known username/password combinations against different systems, applications, or services to gain additional authenticated access. Credential Stuffing attacks rely upon the fact that many users leverage the same username/password combination for multiple systems, applications, and services.

records.name: Password Spraying
records.label: AttackPattern
records.description: In a Password Spraying attack, an adversary tries a small list (e.g. 3-5) of common or expected passwords, often matching the target's complexity policy, against a known list of user accounts to gain valid credentials. The adversary tries a particular password for each user account, before moving onto the next password in the list. This approach assists the adversary in remaining undetected by avoiding rapid or frequent account lockouts. The adversary may then reattempt the process with additional passwords, once enough time has passed to prevent inducing a lockout.

records.name: Remote Services with Stolen Credentials
records.label: AttackPattern
records.description: This pattern of attack involves an adversary that uses stolen credentials to leverage remote services such as RDP, telnet, SSH, and VNC to log into a system. Once access is gained, any number of malicious activities could be performed.

records.name: Use of Captured Hashes (Pass The Hash)
records.label: AttackPattern
records.description: An adversary obtains (i.e. steals or purchases) legitimate Windows domain credential hash values to access systems within the domain that leverage the Lan Man (LM) and/or NT Lan Man (NTLM) authentication protocols.

records.name: Password Brute Forcing
records.label: AttackPattern
records.description: An adversary tries every possible value for a password until they succeed. A brute force attack, if feasible computationally, will always be successful because it will essentially go through all possible passwords given the alphabet used (lower case letters, upper case letters, numbers, symbols, etc.) and the maximum length of the password.

records.name: Kerberoasting
records.label: AttackPattern
records.description: Through the exploitation of how service accounts leverage Kerberos authentication with Service Principal Names (SPNs), the adversary obtains and subsequently cracks the hashed credentials of a service account target to exploit its privileges. The Kerberos authentication protocol centers around a ticketing system which is used to request/grant access to services and to then access the requested services. As an authenticated user, the adversary may request Active Directory and obtain a service ticket with portions encrypted via RC4 with the private key of the authenticated account. By extracting… (+126 chars)

records.name: Use of Captured Tickets (Pass The Ticket)
records.label: AttackPattern
records.description: An adversary uses stolen Kerberos tickets to access systems/resources that leverage the Kerberos authentication protocol. The Kerberos authentication protocol centers around a ticketing system which is used to request/grant access to services and to then access the requested services. An adversary can obtain any one of these tickets (e.g. Service Ticket, Ticket Granting Ticket, Silver Ticket, or Golden Ticket) to authenticate to a system/resource without needing the account's credentials. results.query: MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 300
